Key Characteristics & Etiology: Bleeding from erosion of mucosal defect into submucosal vessels; caused by H. pylori infection or chronic NSAID/aspirin use.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Acid-peptic ulceration penetrates gastroduodenal arterial branches (e.g. gastroduodenal artery in posterior duodenal wall).
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Hematemesis (coffee-ground or frank blood), melena, orthostatic hypotension, tachycardia. Red Flag: Hemodynamic instability.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Flexible Upper GI Endoscopy (OGDS). Management: Resuscitation, IV PPI, dual endoscopic therapy (Adrenaline injection + Clips/Thermal), H. pylori eradication.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Dilated submucosal veins in distal esophagus secondary to portal hypertension (cirrhosis, portal vein thrombosis).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Increased portal venous pressure (>10 mmHg) diverts blood into portosystemic collateral plexus at gastroesophageal junction.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Sudden massive painless hematemesis, melena, stigmata of chronic liver disease, hemorrhagic shock.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Emergency OGDS. Management: Immediate Terlipressin/Octreotide, Endoscopic Variceal Band Ligation (EVL), Sengstaken-Blakemore tube if refractory, TIPS.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Malignant epithelial tumor of middle/upper esophagus; risk factors include smoking, alcohol, betel nut, caustic strictures.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Transmural tumor expansion lacks outer serosal wall protection, causing early local lymphatic and mediastinal invasion.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Progressive dysphagia (solids then liquids), rapid weight loss, regurgitation. Red Flag: Hoarseness, odynophagia, Virchow's node.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: OGDS with biopsy (gold standard); CT Thorax/Abdomen for staging. Management: Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy + Esophagectomy (Ivor Lewis / McKeown).

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Malignant tumor arising in lower third esophagus; strongly linked to chronic GERD, Barrett's Esophagus, and central obesity.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Chronic acid/bile reflux causes intestinal metaplasia of distal esophageal squamous epithelium to columnar epithelium (Barrett's).
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Progressive dysphagia, retrosternal burning pain, weight loss, anorexia. Red Flag: Hematemesis, supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: OGDS with biopsy; Endoscopic Ultrasound (EUS) for T/N staging. Management: Multimodal neoadjuvant therapy + Surgical resection (Esophagectomy).

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Neurodegenerative motility disorder of distal esophagus occurring in young adults (20-40 yrs).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Degeneration of inhibitory ganglion cells in myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus leads to hypertonic, non-relaxing LES and aperistalsis.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Progressive dysphagia to BOTH solids and liquids simultaneously, regurgitation of undigested food, nocturnal cough, retrosternal chest pain.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: High-Resolution Manometry (gold standard: elevated IRP > 15 mmHg); Barium swallow ('bird's-beak' sign). Management: Laparoscopic Heller's cardiomyotomy + Dor/Toupet fundoplication.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Malignant tumor of stomach mucosa; Intestinal (H. pylori, salt/nitrates) vs. Diffuse type (signet-ring cells, E-cadherin loss).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Malignant ulceration or linitis plastica ('leather-bottle' stomach) leading to local transmural growth and peritoneal seeding.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Early dyspepsia, early satiety, epigastric pain, weight loss. Red Flag: Virchow's node, Krukenberg tumor (ovarian), Blumer's shelf.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: OGDS + multiple biopsies; CT Abdomen/Pelvis. Management: Radical Subtotal or Total Gastrectomy + D2 lymphadenectomy + Chemotherapy.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Mechanical obstruction of pyloric channel due to chronic duodenal ulcer cicatrization or Ca Pyloric Antrum.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Fibrotic scarring or malignant tissue expansion blocks pyloric outflow, causing extreme gastric distension.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Profuse, non-bilious projectile vomiting of undigested food, succussion splash, dehydration, weight loss.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: OGDS; Hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria on ABG. Management: NG suction, IV Normal Saline + KCl, Endoscopic balloon dilation or Gastrojejunostomy.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Full-thickness ulcer perforation (anterior wall of 1st part of duodenum) secondary to H. pylori or chronic NSAID use.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Transmural gastric/duodenal ulceration leaks caustic acidic contents into peritoneal cavity, causing chemical peritonitis.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Sudden agonizing 'thunderclap' epigastric pain, generalized board-like abdominal rigidity, loss of liver dullness, absent bowel sounds.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Erect Chest X-ray (free gas under diaphragm / pneumoperitoneum in >75%). Management: Emergency resuscitation, IV PPI, Cellan-Jones / Graham pedicled omental patch repair.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Mucosal tear at gastroesophageal junction triggered by severe vomiting/retching (frequently post-alcohol binge).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Sudden increase in intra-abdominal pressure stretches and tears the non-compliant GE junction mucosa/submucosa.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Episode of non-bloody retching/vomiting immediately followed by hematemesis, epigastric discomfort.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: OGDS showing longitudinal mucosal tear across GE junction. Management: Supportive, IV PPI; endoscopic adrenaline injection or hemoclips if bleeding persists.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Spontaneous transmural barogenic rupture of distal esophagus caused by violent retching/vomiting against closed glottis.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Sudden increase in intraluminal pressure causes full-thickness tear of left posterolateral lower esophagus into pleural cavity.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Mackler's Triad: Vomiting, severe lower chest/epigastric pain, and subcutaneous emphysema; rapidly leads to sepsis and septic shock.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: CT Chest with oral water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin); Chest X-ray (pleural effusion, pneumomediastinum). Management: Emergency surgical repair / T-tube drainage / stenting + broad-spectrum antibiotics.
